title: The Secure Shell (SSH) Transport Layer Protocol

hero.subtitle: The transport layer of SSH that provides encrypted remote access, replacing telnet and rlogin as the standard for secure server administration.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The SSH Transport Layer Protocol provides server authentication, confidentiality, and integrity over an insecure network. It is the foundation for the SSH connection and authentication protocols.

SSH is one of the most important tools in a system administrator's toolkit. It provides secure remote shell access, file transfer (SCP/SFTP), port forwarding, and is the transport for Git over SSH.
sections.eli5: Telnet is like shouting your password across a crowded room. SSH first goes into a private booth, checks that it is the right booth, and only then starts talking.

sections.title: Key Exchange
sections.content:
SSH uses a key exchange algorithm to establish shared secrets for encryption and MAC computation. RFC 4253 itself defines only the two Diffie-Hellman methods with SHA-1 (group1 and group14); the methods below are later additions that modern implementations prefer.

diffie-hellman-group14-sha256DH with 2048-bit group, SHA-256 hash
curve25519-sha256ECDH on Curve25519 - modern default
ecdh-sha2-nistp256ECDH on NIST P-256 curve

The key exchange also verifies the server's identity via its host key. On first connection, the client stores the host key fingerprint ("known_hosts"). This is the famous "Are you sure you want to continue connecting?" prompt.
sections.eli5: The two computers each mix a private number into a public number and swap the results. Anyone listening sees only the mixed paint, but both ends can recover the same secret colour. The server also signs the exchange to prove it is the real one.

sections.title: Encryption and MAC
sections.content:
After key exchange, all traffic is encrypted with a symmetric cipher and integrity-protected with a MAC or AEAD:

Algorithm
Type
chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com
AEAD (recommended)
aes128-gcm@openssh.com
AEAD
aes256-ctr
Cipher (paired with a separate MAC)
sections.eli5: Once they share a secret, everything is locked in a box that only the two of them can open, and each box has a tamper seal so they can tell if someone fiddled with it.

sections.title: Host Keys
sections.content:
Server host keys verify the server's identity and prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.

Ed25519
Modern, fast, small keys - the recommended host key type
ECDSA
Elliptic curve keys on NIST curves - widely supported
RSA
Legacy but universal support - use SHA-256 signatures (rsa-sha2-256)
Checking a Host Key Fingerprint
$ ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
256 SHA256:AbC123... root@server (ED25519)
sections.eli5: Every server has its own signature. The first time you visit, your computer writes down what the signature looks like. Next time, if the signature looks different, it warns you that someone may be pretending.

subtitle: The transport layer of SSH that provides encrypted remote access, replacing telnet and rlogin as the standard for secure server administration.

tldr.problem: Remote login with telnet and rlogin sent passwords and every keystroke as plain text that anyone on the path could read or change.
tldr.mechanism: The two sides swap version strings, agree on algorithms with SSH_MSG_KEXINIT, run a Diffie-Hellman key exchange in which the server signs the result with its host key, then switch to encrypted, integrity-protected binary packets.
tldr.outcome: A private, tamper-evident connection with an authenticated server, ready for the SSH authentication and connection protocols to run inside it.

eli5.summary: Before you tell a computer your password, SSH first builds a secret tunnel to it. The two computers agree on a secret code without ever sending the secret itself, and the server shows proof of who it is.

today: The algorithms this RFC marks as required have aged badly: diffie-hellman-group1-sha1, 3des-cbc and ssh-dss are disabled or removed in current OpenSSH. The framing, the version exchange, KEXINIT negotiation and the host-key-signed exchange hash are all unchanged. Newer RFCs extend the algorithm lists, for example Curve25519 key exchange (RFC 8731), Ed25519 host keys (RFC 8709) and SHA-2 Diffie-Hellman groups (RFC 8268), and OpenSSH adds its own chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com cipher.

messages.label: SSH-2.0-softwareversion
messages.note: Identification string ending in CR LF. Both sides send one as soon as the TCP connection opens.

messages.label: SSH-2.0-softwareversion
messages.note: The server may send other text lines first, but none may begin with "SSH-".

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXINIT (20)
messages.note: Random cookie plus ordered lists of supported algorithms.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXINIT (20)
messages.note: The first client-listed algorithm the server also supports wins.

messages.label: Diffie-Hellman value e
messages.note: SSH_MSG_KEXDH_INIT carries e = g^x mod p.

messages.label: Host key K_S, value f, signature of H
messages.note: SSH_MSG_KEXDH_REPLY. The signature covers the exchange hash H.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS (21)
messages.note: Everything the sender transmits after this uses the new keys.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS (21)
messages.note: Encryption and MAC are now in force in both directions.

data.title: SSH_MSG_KEXINIT payload
data.code:
byte         SSH_MSG_KEXINIT
byte[16]     cookie (random bytes)
name-list    kex_algorithms
name-list    server_host_key_algorithms
name-list    encryption_algorithms_client_to_server
name-list    encryption_algorithms_server_to_client
name-list    mac_algorithms_client_to_server
name-list    mac_algorithms_server_to_client
name-list    compression_algorithms_client_to_server
name-list    compression_algorithms_server_to_client
name-list    languages_client_to_server
name-list    languages_server_to_client
boolean      first_kex_packet_follows
uint32       0 (reserved for future extension)

data.title: Binary packet format
data.code:
uint32    packet_length
byte      padding_length
byte[n1]  payload; n1 = packet_length - padding_length - 1
byte[n2]  random padding; n2 = padding_length
byte[m]   mac (Message Authentication Code); m = mac_length

# packet_length excludes the mac and itself.
# packet_length || padding_length || payload || padding must be a
# multiple of the cipher block size or 8, whichever is larger.
# At least 4 and at most 255 bytes of padding.
